text:
**Yes, the cable can be the limiting factor.** Charging speed is set by the weakest link among the charger, the cable, and the device. USB-IF notes that a certified cable doesn't add to the capabilities of the products it connects ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)).

**What the ratings mean**
- **60W cable:** 20V at 3A. This is enough for phones, tablets, and most small laptops.
- **100W cable:** 20V at 5A. This is the older rating. USB-IF replaced it with the 240W cable in the Type-C spec (Release 2.1) and stopped certifying 100W cables on December 22, 2021. You may still own one or see one for sale, but new certified cables are only 60W or 240W ([USB-IF Compliance Updates](https://compliance.usb.org/index.asp?Format=Standard&UpdateFile=Cables+and+Connectors&pubDate=20261005), [UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations)).
- **240W cable:** 48V at 5A, using USB PD 3.1's Extended Power Range. Higher voltage steps (28V, 36V, 48V) give 140W, 180W, and 240W ([USB-IF USB PD](https://www.usb.org/usb-charger-pd)). These cables must have an E-marker chip ([UL Solutions](https://www.ul.com/insights/240w-usb-c-cable-performance-testing-and-safety-considerations)).

**When it matters**
- **Phone or tablet:** a 60W cable won't slow you down.
- **Laptop that draws more than 60W, with a charger that can supply it:** a 60W cable will cap charging at 60W, so you'd need a 100W-class or 240W cable.
- **Device or charger already under 60W:** the cable makes no difference.
- A higher-rated cable never hurts. A 240W cable works fine with a 30W charger, and the charger and device just negotiate the lower power.

**How to check yours**
- Look for a printed 60W or 240W logo on the cable or its packaging. USB-IF requires certified USB-C to USB-C cables to carry one of these power markings, plus a data-rate marking (except USB 2.0 cables) ([USB-IF](https://www.usb.org/cable_connector)).
- Check whether it's certified. USB-IF has a searchable list of logo-certified products: [usb.org/products](https://www.usb.org/products).
- If the cable has no markings, assume 60W or less. This is my own inference, since the sources only cover how certified cables are labeled. Also note that USB 2.0-only "charging" cables can still be rated for 60W while being slow for data.

If you tell me your charger and device (for example, a 100W laptop charger and a specific laptop), I can say which rating you need and look for specific cables to link.
